title: Lateral Elbow Tendinopathy (Tennis Elbow)
case: Case: A 46-year-old mechanic has 4 months of right outer elbow pain when gripping tools and lifting parts. Tenderness is at the lateral epicondyle. Cozen test reproduces his pain, and grip strength is lower on the right with pain. Elbow range is full. Neck and neurological screens are normal. No red flags.

Working diagnosis: lateral elbow tendinopathy. Plan: education, change tool grip and lifting technique, isometric then progressive wrist extension and grip loading over about 12 weeks, optional forearm strap, reassess every 3 to 4 weeks, and avoid steroid injection as a first step.

differentials.name: Radial tunnel syndrome
differentials.key: Deeper, more distal forearm pain, pain on resisted supination or middle finger extension, little epicondyle tenderness
differentials.next: Nerve-focused care, medical review if persistent

differentials.name: Posterolateral rotatory instability
differentials.key: History of dislocation or injury, clicking, apprehension

qa: Why is a corticosteroid injection not a first choice? It may give short-term relief, but studies show worse results and more recurrence at about one year.

How do you tell tennis elbow from radial tunnel syndrome? Tennis elbow is tender at the epicondyle, while radial tunnel pain is deeper and more distal, with pain on resisted supination or middle finger extension.
Why test the neck? Cervical root problems can refer pain to the outer elbow and forearm, and treating the elbow alone would not help.
Why measure pain-free grip? It is a simple, repeatable baseline of function that shows progress.
Why reduce rather than stop gripping tasks? Complete rest lowers load capacity, while gradual loading rebuilds it.

fields.Position: Sitting with the elbow bent to about 90 degrees and supported
fields.Action: Press on the lateral epicondyle and the area just in front of and below it, where the extensor tendon attaches
fields.Positive: Localised tenderness that reproduces the familiar pain
fields.Limits: Tenderness is also present with other conditions, so combine with load tests

fields.Purpose: Load the wrist extensors to see whether the outer elbow pain is reproduced
fields.Position: Sitting; elbow bent to about 90 degrees, forearm pronated, fist closed
fields.Therapist position: Beside the patient, one hand supports the elbow and palpates the lateral epicondyle, the other hand holds the back of the patient's hand
fields.Action: The patient extends the wrist and radially deviates it against the therapist's resistance, while the therapist keeps palpating the epicondyle
fields.Positive: Sharp familiar pain at the lateral epicondyle
fields.Errors: Resisting at the fingers, not the hand; applying force too quickly

fields.Action: Passively flex the wrist fully while keeping the elbow straight and the forearm pronated

fields.Position: Sitting, elbow extended, forearm pronated, fingers extended
fields.Action: The patient extends the middle finger against resistance applied to the top of the finger

redFlags.Finding: Fall or injury with swelling, inability to straighten or rotate the arm
Hot, red, swollen elbow with fever
Progressive weakness or wasting, numbness in the hand or fingers
Constant night pain, weight loss, a lump
Multiple swollen painful joints with morning stiffness
Sudden loss of grip with a gap at the tendon
Chest pain, sweating, breathlessness with arm pain

manual.name: Mobilization with movement (Mulligan lateral glide)
manual.why: May give short-term pain relief and improve pain-free grip
manual.finding: Pain on gripping that eases with the technique
manual.application: Sitting with the elbow extended; the therapist applies a lateral glide to the forearm just below the elbow, the patient grips, and repeat several times
manual.stop: The technique does not reduce pain immediately, or pain increases

manual.name: Soft-tissue work for the forearm
manual.application: Gentle sustained pressure on the muscle belly, not heavy pressure on the tender tendon

manualNotes: Preferred starting choice: education, load management and progressive loading. Manual therapy is optional for short-term relief, and the effect is generally small. Do not use deep friction massage as the main treatment. Do not claim to break up scar tissue.

exercise.Steps: Sit with the forearm on a table, palm down; the patient holds the wrist in extension while resisted lightly by the other hand
exercise.Starting dose: 5 holds of 30 to 45 seconds, once or twice a day

exercise.Exercise: Wrist extension with a light dumbbell, slow tempo; supination and pronation with a hammer or weight
exercise.Steps: Raise the wrist for about 3 seconds, lower for about 3 seconds

exercise.Exercise: Heavier wrist extension, reverse curls, towel or putty grip, farmer's carry
exercise.Progress when: Pain stays at about 3 to 4 out of 10 or less and no flare the next day

exercise.Exercise: Racket or tool work simulation, lifting tasks, return to sport

exerciseNotes: Principle: tendon loading is the core treatment. A short period of isometric holds to calm pain, then progressive strengthening of the wrist extensors, grip and the whole arm. Several exercise types appear helpful, and adherence matters most.
Eccentric exercise with a flexible rubber bar (twist exercise): some trials suggest benefit. It is optional, and the patient should find it comfortable.
Symptom rule: pain up to about 3 to 4 out of 10 during exercise that settles within 24 hours is acceptable. Pain that stays higher into the next day means reduce load.

Load management and ergonomics: reduce, rather than stop, painful gripping and lifting. Change tool handles to a larger grip, keep the wrist neutral, lift with the palm up when possible, use both hands, take breaks, and adjust mouse and keyboard setup.
Bracing: a forearm counterforce strap just below the elbow may reduce pain with gripping for some people in the short term. Wrist splints are not routine.
modalityNotes: Medical options (decided by doctors): corticosteroid injection may reduce pain in the short term, but studies show worse outcomes at longer follow-up (about a year) compared with waiting or physiotherapy, and higher recurrence. Platelet-rich plasma injections do not show consistent benefit. Surgery is rare and for persistent severe cases.
pathway: Any emergency or urgent flag? Yes: act as in Section G.
Neck or nerve source suspected? Use the cervical or nerve pathway.
Outer elbow pain, epicondyle tenderness, pain on resisted wrist or middle finger extension, normal elbow range? Yes: working diagnosis is lateral elbow tendinopathy.
Pain over the radial tunnel or posterior interosseous nerve signs? Consider radial tunnel syndrome, alone or together.
Begin education, load management and progressive loading.
If there is no improvement after a full trial, review the diagnosis and consider medical options.
Visit 1: screen flags, neck and nerve sources, explain the condition and its usual course, set goals.
Early: reduce painful gripping, start isometrics, consider a strap and manual therapy for comfort.
